claim_assessments.reason: The source frames the cost/benefit question and reports total runtimes. None of the examined chunks contains a synchronized-timing, tiny-scale, MPS, cost-accounted screen. Absence from these chunks is not novelty; outside this pack it is unknown.

evidence.supports: Low-rank factorization of K_gamma is named as future work.
A structured K approximation is already used for the MLP contraction.

claim_assessments.reason: The source names the low-rank family but does not specify the eigen-plus-isotropic-remainder form. The proposal itself calls this a known approximation and not new. That is consistent with the examined evidence, but the specific form is not located in these chunks.

C3 is an unobserved expected result, not evidence. Its wording is also inconsistent with the rest of the proposal. 'At most 3% gain' conflicts with the hypothesis (≤0.97× time, i.e. at least a 3% gain) and with the kill threshold (≥3% better). The source reports only that Newton–Muon is more than 4% faster than Muon, at 124M+ scale on GPU. No examined chunk reports a low-rank-vs-full comparison.

mechanism_check.assumption_scope: Source assumptions: activations K are strongly anisotropic in Pythia-70M; k in {16,32,64} works best at 124M–455M; damping gamma·tr(K)/n is used; settings are single H100/L40S. Target assumptions: a tiny d≤512 Transformer on MPS; the top-r spectrum dominates; refresh plus preconditioning is a material fraction of step time. Tiny scale and MPS are an excluded or untested regime, not a contradiction. The source's statement that the overhead is 'insignificant' is evidence against the target premise f>5%, not a contradiction of it.
mechanism_check.specialized_operation: 1) K←βK+(1−β)ZZᵀ/N. 2) γ_ℓ=γ·tr(K)/n. 3) At refresh, compute (V,Λ)=top-r eig(K) and ρ=(trK−ΣΛ)/(n−r). 4) Set D=(Λ+γ_ℓI)^{-1}−(ρ+γ_ℓ)^{-1}I and c=(ρ+γ_ℓ)^{-1}. 5) Each step compute G̃=((G V) D) Vᵀ + c G. This costs 2mnr+mn flops, versus mn² for G K^{-1}. 6) Run momentum, then NS5, then the update. The algebra checks: r=n reproduces (K+γI)^{-1}, and r=0 gives cG, which is Muon after msgn. The damping detail matters. Because γ_ℓ equals 0.2× the mean eigenvalue, the tail eigenvalues λ_i≪γ_ℓ are already nearly flattened to 1/γ_ℓ. Replacing them by ρ therefore changes the operator only on mid-spectrum directions. This is plausible, but it must be measured.
mechanism_check.remaining_effect: The per-step apply saves flops only when 2r<n. The refresh cost is a separate issue. A full eigh is O(n³) and usually slower than Cholesky, so a refresh saving requires r-step subspace iteration at O(n²r·iters). On MPS, the availability and speed of eigh or Cholesky kernels (possible CPU fallback) is unverified and could reverse the sign of any saving. The surviving effect is therefore a pure wall-clock trade-off with fidelity loss. Whether any saving exceeds noise at n≤512 is unresolved.
mechanism_check.simplest_baseline: Full-inverse Newton–Muon in three variants. (a) Larger k: zero code, but staleness. (b) The source's polynomial-iteration inverse (Appendix B.3): matmul-only, MPS-friendly, still O(n³) per refresh. (c) Block-diagonal K (Appendix A). Plain Muon is the zero-overhead floor. Baseline (b) is the most direct competitor for cutting refresh cost, and the proposal omits it.
mechanism_check.distinguishing_test: Profile one optimizer step on MPS with torch.mps.synchronize, separating forward/backward, refresh (Cholesky, eigh or subspace iteration, and polynomial inverse) and apply (G K^{-1} vs. the low-rank apply) across n∈{256,512} and r∈{16,32,64}. Run the costly training sweep only if the full-inverse overhead fraction f exceeds 5% and the low-rank path is faster than both Cholesky and the polynomial inverse. In parallel, compute the operator error ‖P−(K+γI)^{-1}‖ relative to (K+γI)^{-1} on logged K matrices, and the cosine between msgn(G P) and msgn(G K^{-1}).

review.reason: The operator algebra is correct and reduces properly at r=n and r=0, so this is not a no-op. The idea is coherent but uncertain on cost. At tiny n, the apply saving requires 2r<n, and the refresh saving requires avoiding a full eigh. The source already states the overhead is insignificant, and that it is only a few percent of total runtime at larger scale. The proposal also omits the polynomial-inverse and larger-k baselines as cost competitors. Its C3 wording ('at most 3% gain') is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis and kill threshold and should be corrected. A cheap profiling test decides the question before any training.

evidence.supports: The baseline inverse options include a polynomial iteration, which is an omitted cost competitor.
The polynomial inverse is a cheaper existing alternative.
Damping flattens the spectrum, which is relevant to how closely an isotropic remainder can match the full inverse.
Spectral concentration is shown in the source model only, not in the target model.

review.strongest_counterargument: The test may be redundant. At d≤512, a Cholesky inverse every 32 steps plus one 512×512 matmul per step is likely well under 1% of step time, and the source itself calls the cost insignificant. Profiling may simply confirm that there is nothing to save. Conversely, if MPS lacks efficient eigh or Cholesky, the low-rank path could be slower, not faster.
review.required_test: A synchronized MPS microbenchmark of overhead fraction f for three refresh methods (Cholesky, polynomial inverse, rank-r subspace iteration) and two apply methods (full and low-rank), plus operator and msgn-direction fidelity on logged K. Kill the project if f<5% or if the low-rank path is not faster than the polynomial inverse.
